title: Rig — Network
description: Who is using the link, where it goes, and whether it is full. The queue panels answer the question throughput cannot: why everything lags while a download sits under its own speed cap.

panels.title: Down
panels.description: The default-route interface alone. Container bridges, VMs and the tailnet carry bytes that never reach the ISP.

panels.title: Of the line
panels.description: Downlink against RIG_NET_DOWN_MBIT.

defaults.noValue: No line speed set. RIG_NET_DOWN_MBIT in .env, then this reads against what you pay for instead of against the busiest minute so far.

panels.title: Of its own best
panels.description: Against the fastest this line has been seen to go in 7 days. The stand-in while nobody has typed in what it was sold as.

panels.title: Queue
panels.description: A link is never slow, it is full. When it is full the bytes still arrive at the same rate and every interactive packet waits behind them, so the honest measure of 'the internet is laggy' is round-trip time against its own idle value, not throughput. 1.0 is an idle path. Above 4 the lag is real and it is not the download rate that caused it.

panels.title: Loss
panels.description: Echoes that never came back. To the gateway it is the radio or the cable; only past it is it the ISP.

panels.title: Named owner
panels.description: Share of the link's bytes this stack can attribute to a process group. The rest is UDP without conntrack accounting, and connections too short to be sampled. `rig net doctor` says which.

panels.title: Down, by process group
panels.description: Internet only, and named by the same groups as every other dashboard. Defined in process-exporter/config.yml.

panels.title: Up, by process group
panels.description: The uplink is usually the smaller pipe, and filling it queues the acknowledgements every download depends on. A backup or a sync client here slows a machine that is downloading nothing.

panels.title: Link against what has an owner
panels.description: The gap is UDP with no conntrack accounting plus connections that opened and closed between two samples. Measured, not assumed.

panels.title: Total by process group
panels.description: Everything recorded, per group. A cumulative counter, so this is the whole history the exporter has watched.

panels.title: Round trip time against its own idle value
panels.description: A link is never slow, it is full. When it is full the bytes still arrive at the same rate and every interactive packet waits behind them, so the honest measure of 'the internet is laggy' is round-trip time against its own idle value, not throughput. The floor line is the best this path has answered in since the exporter started. Distance between the two lines is somebody else's queue.

panels.title: Queue factor
panels.description: Round trip over idle round trip. This is the panel to open when a download is capped and the machine still feels slow — the cap limits the rate, not the queue the router builds.

panels.title: Loss and retransmits
panels.description: TCP retransmits rise before ICMP loss does: a full queue drops the bulk flow's packets first, which is exactly the traffic nobody notices.

panels.title: Worst round trip per process group
panels.description: Taken from each group's own established connections, so a game and a download on the same link can be told apart. A game climbing here is the complaint, whatever the download is doing.

panels.title: Down, by remote address
panels.description: Addresses beyond the busiest fold into `other`. `rig net peers` resolves names.

panels.title: By service
panels.description: Named from the remote port. A number instead of a name means a port nobody has agreed on, which is normal for peer-to-peer and for games.

panels.title: Busiest peers now
panels.description: Instant rate to each address. `rig net conns` has the per-connection detail, which is deliberately never a metric — one series per socket would cost more than the rest of this stack together.

panels.title: Every interface, down
panels.description: Bridges and virtual interfaces included. Docker gives one bridge per compose project, so a busy line here that is not the default route never left the machine.

panels.title: Wifi signal
panels.description: Above -60 dBm is strong, below -72 the radio steps down to slow rates and the link is the bottleneck before any queue is.

defaults.noValue: No wireless interface — this machine is on a cable.

panels.title: Wifi retries
panels.description: Frames the radio had to send again. Airtime spent on nothing, and it rises long before throughput falls.

panels.title: Errors and drops
panels.description: Drops on a virtual interface are ordinary. Drops on the default route are not.

panels.title: Established connections
panels.description: A group holding hundreds of connections is either a peer-to-peer client or a download accelerator, and both defeat any single-connection rate cap.

panels.title: Name resolution
panels.description: Time for a name to become an address, through the same path an application uses. Slow here with a quiet link is the resolver, not the line.
